base.anonce: What is a sitemap and how to set it up. Common practices and example files.

content.text: A sitemap is an html page of a site or a special xml file that contains links to all important pages of the site. It is similar to a book table of contents, helping visitors and search robots quickly find pages with minimal transitions.

Search robots index the site gradually, starting from the main page. With deep nesting, indexing all pages can take a long time. A sitemap provides direct links to pages, speeding up the process. There are three types: HTML, XML, and TXT.
An HTML sitemap is a page listing the most important sections and pages of the site.

blocks.text: The HTML sitemap is designed for users rather than robots, helping people navigate quickly.
Do not place more than 100 links on one HTML sitemap page.

content.text: HTML sitemaps often use tree structures with sections and subsections. In practice, all footer, header, and body links form an HTML sitemap.

blocks.text: An HTML sitemap has little value to search engines compared to XML.

content.text: For large sites, it is necessary to use an XML sitemap, which contains structured data about each page.

blocks.text: An XML sitemap is a file named sitemap.xml at the root of a site. It can contain up to 50,000 links.
If a sitemap exceeds 50,000 links or 10 MB, split it into several files and use <sitemapindex>.

content.text: TXT sitemap is a simple text file listing all links line by line.

blocks.text: Max 50,000 links, no <lastmod> or priority attributes.
Search engines may not strictly follow your set priorities.

content.text: The sitemap file should be located at the root of the site. Search engines can find it, but you can also provide direct links.
